extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of scientific method, experimentalists, and philosophers of science
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for performing inductive inquiry and experimental investigation: how to observe, design experiments, and infer causal relations using methods like the Method of Agreement and Method of Difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental analysis and decomposition of phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: The observer must mentally decompose complex phenomena into their component antecedents and consequents before attempting to determine causal relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mental partition is an indispensable first step: see what parts a thing is composed of, carry subdivision far enough to know what observations or experiments are required, and remain ready to subdivide further as occasion requires. Beware inattention, conflating imagination/inference with observation, poor granularity (throwing distinct things together or splitting what should be considered one), and leaving quantities vague. These rules are rules of self-education to prepare the mind to observe, not an art that directly performs observation for you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vary the circumstances (Baconian rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: To assign which antecedents produce which consequents, follow the rule of varying the circumstances: meet antecedents apart from each other or find consequents apart from other consequents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two complementary ways to vary circumstances: find instances in nature where the desired antecedent or consequent occurs separately (observation), or artificially produce the instance by arranging circumstances (experiment). The value of an instance depends on its intrinsic suitability; the logical employment of such instances is the same whether found or made. This is the foundation of experimental inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation versus experiment — choose appropriate mode
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation ('finding' instances in nature) and Experiment ('making' instances by artificial arrangement) are logically equivalent in principle but differ greatly in practice and power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiment extends observation by producing variations not available in nature and by allowing control over concomitant circumstances. Observation is often the only resource when the effect is known but the cause is not, but it can usually only establish sequences and co-existences, not causation. In sciences where experiments are impossible or limited (astronomy, social science, parts of physiology), induction by direct experience is at a disadvantage and deductive methods play a larger role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolation and control in experiment
rubrics_metrics.description: When a phenomenon can be produced artificially, place it among known circumstances so you can control and vary concomitant factors to observe what changes the phenomenon produces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produce the agent under precisely known conditions (e.g., electric machine producing electric phenomena) so you can introduce one well-defined circumstance after another and observe responses. This allows production of many combinations and assessment of behavior under varied conditions. Beware that the means used to produce a change might themselves cause effects; such possibilities should be tested by additional experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: FIRST CANON — Method of Agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: If two or more instances of the phenomenon under investigation have only one circumstance in common, the circumstance in which alone all the instances agree, is the cause (or effect) of the given phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply by comparing different instances in which the phenomenon occurs; whatever is common to all is an invariable antecedent or consequent. Examples: combining an oil and an alkali producing soap; crystallization always accompanied by deposition from a liquid. Limitation: Agreement can establish an invariable antecedent/consequent but does not alone prove causation — the invariable antecedent might be itself an effect of some other cause (day and night analogy). To prove causation you generally need to produce the antecedent and observe the effect (i.e., use Method of Difference/experiment).

rubrics_metrics.name: SECOND CANON — Method of Difference
rubrics_metrics.description: If an instance in which the phenomenon occurs, and an instance in which it does not occur, have every circumstance in common save one — that one occurring only in the former — the circumstance in which alone the two instances differ, is the effect, or the cause, or an indispensable part of the cause, of the phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare a matched pair of instances identical except for the presence/absence of one circumstance; the differing circumstance is implicated as cause/effect. This method is more strictly defined and especially suited to artificial experiment, because experiments can produce the required near-identity of instances. Example: knowing a man was alive just before and dead immediately after a gunshot establishes the shot as cause (when all else is equal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Elimination principle underlying agreement and difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental inquiry proceeds by successive exclusion of accompanying circumstances to discover which are causally connected to the phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Axiom: whatever circumstances can be excluded without prejudice to the phenomenon are not connected causally; whatever cannot be excluded is connected by a law. Method of Agreement eliminates non-essential factors by cross-instance comparison; Method of Difference identifies indispensable factors by comparing occurrence vs non-occurrence under otherwise identical circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method selection and certainty about causation
rubrics_metrics.description: Method of Difference is the means by which direct experience can, with certainty, establish causes; Method of Agreement identifies invariable relations but is insufficient alone to establish causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Method of Difference (controlled contrasts) wherever practicable to attain causal certainty. Use Method of Agreement for sciences or cases where experiments are impossible, but treat conclusions as provisional until the antecedent can be produced and tested. Recognize that spontaneous natural instances rarely satisfy the tight similarity required by Method of Difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start from the known and proceed to the unknown
rubrics_metrics.description: You can only travel from known to unknown — choose to begin your inquiry from whichever end (cause or effect) you are best acquainted with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the agent (cause) is familiar, vary it and observe effects; if the effect is familiar but causes obscure, compare instances of the effect to seek common antecedents. Practical limitation: when beginning from the effect, artificial experiments to produce antecedents are usually unavailable, so conclusions are less certain without reversal (producing antecedent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Confirm observational inductions by producing the antecedent
rubrics_metrics.description: An invariable antecedent discovered by observation is not proven to be the cause until the antecedent is artificially produced under known circumstances and the effect follows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if observation shows an antecedent always present with an effect, reverse the proof by producing the antecedent (when possible) and observing the effect. Examples: producing charged water to form quartz crystals or producing cooling under pressure to make artificial marble. Without such reversal, the observed invariable antecedent might be a concomitant or be produced by some ulterior cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical cautions for complex or non-reproducible phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: In domains where artificial experimentation is impossible or subjects are complex (human minds, societies, astronomy, much of natural history), direct induction has severe limits and may be impracticable for establishing causal laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that natural instances are tangled with innumerable, often unascertainable concomitants; comprehensive analysis of antecedents may be infeasible. In such fields, methods must rely more on deduction and careful comparative observation, and conclusions should be held tentatively. Repeat observations where possible and seek other lines of evidence.
